title: Atomic‐Scale Insights Into the Thermal Stability of High‐Entropy Nanoalloys

recollection.starting_material: Guess: High‐entropy nanoalloys synthesized from a mixture of multiple metal precursors (e.g., equimolar ratios of transition metals) formed into nanoparticles.
recollection.intervention: Guess: The study likely employed thermal annealing (possibly in situ TEM heating experiments) to systematically elevate temperatures and monitor structural changes.
recollection.structure: Guess: The nanoalloys maintained a single‐phase, chemically homogeneous solid‐solution structure at the atomic scale, with minimal phase segregation even at elevated temperatures.
recollection.mechanism: Guess: The high configurational entropy of mixing and sluggish diffusion effects are proposed as the key factors that stabilize the alloy structure at high temperatures, suppressing phase separation and grain growth.
recollection.results: Guess: The paper probably reported that the high-entropy nanoalloys exhibit excellent thermal stability, retaining their structure up to temperatures around 700–900°C, with quantitative measures such as very low diffusion coefficients (on the order of 10^(-20)–10^(-19) m²/s) in the alloy phase.

score.note: The recollection generically identifies elevated-temperature/in situ TEM heating but omits the specific 298–973 K protocol, vacuum conditions, STEM, and simulations. It incorrectly claims homogeneous structural retention, entropy/sluggish-diffusion stabilization, and excellent stability; the paper instead found Au/Cu surface segregation, active diffusion, melting/evaporation at 973 K, and a 22% size reduction.
